title: Mount Identity Audit
user: Developers using Dev Containers or rootless Podman who need to know, before opening a project, whether the workspace bind mount will be readable and writable by the intended remote user.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer describes relying on a locally mounted Dev Container for durable project edits and asks about a MicroVM setup with similar behavior.
A Dev Containers CLI request documents rootless Podman UID mismatches causing Permission denied on workspace bind mounts.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 reports at the container-development boundary; a broken ownership mapping blocks all edits rather than degrading one feature.
current_workaround: Start the container, hit a permission error, then inspect id output and tweak remoteUser, chown commands, or Podman flags by hand.
incumbents_and_gap: Dev Containers CLI, VS Code, Docker, and Podman configure containers, but none gives a small preflight report explaining host UID/GID, remote user, mount ownership, and the exact unsafe mismatch.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI that reads devcontainer.json/Compose metadata, inspects the chosen runtime, and emits a pass/fail ownership table plus safe remediation options. Non-goals: replacing a container runtime, editing host ownership automatically, or provisioning cloud workspaces.
success_measure: In a pilot of 20 repositories, at least 90% of first-run mount permission failures are predicted before container startup.
monetization: free — runtime adapters and trust benefit from an open local diagnostic; paid support can follow.
constraints: Read runtime metadata only by default; never change host file ownership; support Docker and rootless Podman separately; avoid exposing mounted path names in shared reports.
why_distinct: It is an identity-and-mount preflight, not another dev-container launcher or Docker GUI.

title: Run Proof
user: Small application teams with cron jobs and queue workers who need a compact, trustworthy record that scheduled work actually ran and completed, even when CI or dashboard status is misleading.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Laravel operator says uptime checks cannot show whether schedulers fire or workers crash, and asks what teams use to monitor them.
GitHub CLI reported all PR checks passing while a failed check was omitted from its payload, illustrating that a green status is not always evidence of completed work.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 operational reports: background work is invisible to URL uptime checks, and status rollups can be incomplete; missed work has direct customer impact.
current_workaround: Use a ping service, inspect queue dashboards, and manually reconcile application logs after a complaint or a suspiciously green deploy.
incumbents_and_gap: Healthchecks.io, Better Uptime, Laravel Horizon, and GitHub Checks monitor parts of the path; the gap is a portable append-only receipt tying schedule intent, worker heartbeat, completion count, and source status together.
smallest_useful_product: A self-hostable receiver and CLI that accepts signed start/finish heartbeats, imports a CI check snapshot, and renders a one-page missed/late/contradictory-run ledger. Non-goals: queue processing, alert-routing SaaS, or CI replacement.
success_measure: Pilot users identify 95% of intentionally stopped scheduled jobs within one expected run interval and can export a receipt for each alert.
monetization: one-time — a self-hosted reliability record is episodic infrastructure, not a per-event tax.
constraints: Signed ingest endpoints; configurable retention; no job payload retention; clock-skew handling and offline export are required.
why_distinct: It proves execution and exposes contradictory signals instead of offering another generic uptime ping.

title: Clean Env Runner
user: Developers testing workflows locally who need to reproduce a run with an explicit, reviewable environment instead of accidentally inheriting credentials and settings from their shell.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer describing a modern terminal/IDE/agent setup asks what others use and highlights debugging across several local tools.
Act users request host execution without inheriting every parent-process environment variable so local workflow tests do not expose unrelated credentials and session state.

recurrence: The request comes from both day-to-day multi-tool development and local Actions emulation; accidental ambient configuration makes a test irreproducible and can leak credentials.
current_workaround: Open a fresh shell, hand-write env -i commands, maintain several .env files, or hope that CI behaves like a developer laptop.
incumbents_and_gap: direnv, dotenvx, Act, and 1Password inject variables, but they do not make an allowlisted environment and its provenance a repeatable test artifact across arbitrary commands.
smallest_useful_product: A CLI wrapper with declarative allowlists, secret-name placeholders, environment diff previews, and a scrubbed run receipt. Non-goals: storing secrets, replacing CI, or running arbitrary remote code.
success_measure: At least 80% of pilot runs reproduce after a clean-shell restart, with no variable outside the manifest visible to the child process.
monetization: free — an auditable local primitive needs wide adoption; managed policy packs could be paid later.
constraints: Never log secret values; use OS keychain references only; account for Windows, macOS, and Linux process-environment differences.
why_distinct: The product is an explicit environment boundary and receipt, not another dotenv loader.

title: Capacity Sentinel
user: Teams calling one or more model APIs who need early, vendor-neutral evidence of capacity errors, latency regressions, and output-shape degradation before users report failures.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A builder asks how teams detect elevated errors, slow time-to-first-token, timeouts, and silent model drift across LLM APIs.
Gemini CLI's capacity tracking issue centralizes reports of 429 errors and asks for better handling and retry behavior; it has 95 reactions.

recurrence: Independent operator and project-community evidence in 2026, including a 95-reaction capacity issue; provider degradation can be silent until quality or conversion falls.
current_workaround: Watch vendor status pages, aggregate generic HTTP metrics, retry blindly, or notice a change in support tickets.
incumbents_and_gap: Langfuse, Helicone, Datadog, and vendor dashboards provide broad tracing or vendor-specific views; the gap is a privacy-preserving canary suite that measures comparable availability, latency, and structured invariants without retaining prompts.
smallest_useful_product: A self-hostable probe runner that sends user-supplied synthetic canaries, records status/latency/validated JSON invariants, and emits vendor-neutral SLO alerts. Non-goals: proxying production prompts, judging open-ended model quality, or model routing.
success_measure: A pilot detects injected 429 and latency failures within two probe intervals and attributes the affected provider/model with 95% accuracy.
monetization: freemium — a local single-project runner stays free while managed probe locations and retention are paid.
constraints: Synthetic prompts only by default; strict API-key encryption; configurable cost caps; do not claim universal semantic-quality measurement.
why_distinct: It is an SLO canary for externally supplied model endpoints, not an LLM application or tracing wrapper.

title: Agent Audit Ledger
user: Engineers reviewing agent-assisted changes who need an offline, readable record of which files, commands, tests, and delegated tasks produced a patch.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer asks how to validate LLM-generated code when repeated model reviews create noisy findings and manual understanding is expensive.
A Codex regression report says encrypted multi-agent messages removed the readable task audit trail; the issue has 137 reactions.

recurrence: A direct review request and a 137-reaction loss-of-audit-trail report show that reviewability, not code generation alone, is the bottleneck.
current_workaround: Read terminal scrollback, inspect a giant diff, collect screenshots, or ask the agent to narrate work after the fact.
incumbents_and_gap: GitHub PRs, Cursor histories, Claude Code, and Codex expose parts of a session, but there is no portable, tool-neutral signed manifest that connects actions and test evidence to changed files without storing prompts by default.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI/library that consumes simple JSONL action events, hashes touched files, links command exit codes and test artifacts, and exports a Markdown/JSON review ledger. Non-goals: agent orchestration, code generation, or surveillance telemetry.
success_measure: Reviewers answer 'what changed, why, and what was verified' from a ledger in under five minutes for 80% of pilot patches.
monetization: one-time — compliance-conscious teams value local export and predictable ownership.
constraints: Prompt/content capture must be opt-in; redact paths and arguments; cryptographic hashes are metadata, not a guarantee of intent; publish an open event schema.
why_distinct: It turns deterministic execution evidence into a review artifact instead of adding another AI reviewer.

title: Apply Witness
user: Small teams wiring hosted developer platforms who need proof that declared configuration fields were actually accepted and applied, rather than trusting a success message or a partial diff.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A small-team discussion describes the pain of wiring repositories, CI/CD, PRs, packages, and integrations into one hosted platform and the cost of moving later.
Supabase CLI accepted and reported success for an OAuth-server config section while sending none of it; its diff could not reveal the omission.

recurrence: A 2026 small-team platform-lock-in concern and a concrete silent configuration failure point to a high-cost class of false success.
current_workaround: Read provider dashboards after each deploy, compare rendered CLI output manually, or discover a missing setting in production.
incumbents_and_gap: Terraform plans, Pulumi previews, Supabase CLI, and provider dashboards describe desired state; the gap is a lightweight post-apply witness that compares declared fields against provider readback and flags fields that were ignored or normalized away.
smallest_useful_product: A plugin-based CLI with one initial Supabase adapter that records a config input hash, fetches safe readback, and produces field-level applied/unknown/changed receipts. Non-goals: applying configuration, storing provider tokens, or becoming an IaC framework.
success_measure: In a seeded test suite of ignored and normalized fields, the tool marks 100% of non-applied fields as non-successful rather than green.
monetization: one-time — configuration verification is a focused local utility with episodic value.
constraints: Use read-only provider scopes where possible; redact secrets; never infer that an unreadable field is safely applied; adapters must respect provider APIs and terms.
why_distinct: It validates the outcome of an apply, rather than adding another configuration authoring layer.

title: Workspace History Porter
user: People moving between browsers and remote development workspaces who need their task/session index and handoff notes to follow the workspace without making chat history a vendor lock-in.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A team asks how to enable cloud AI development for employees who lack full local environments and need substantial remote compute for tests.
A code-server request notes that messages reside on the server but their browser-local IndexedDB index disappears in a second browser, leaving the same workspace looking empty.

recurrence: Remote-development adoption and a concrete browser-local session-index failure in 2026 make handoff continuity a practical daily problem.
current_workaround: Keep ad-hoc Markdown notes, export chat manually, pin browser tabs, or restart context in each browser.
incumbents_and_gap: code-server, GitHub Codespaces, Coder, and IDE chat tools hold sessions in product-specific stores; the gap is an encrypted, workspace-scoped portable index of task links, handoff notes, and artifact references.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension plus local sidecar that stores an encrypted workspace journal, bookmarks terminal/PR/test URLs, and exports an interoperable handoff file. Non-goals: syncing model transcripts, providing a hosted IDE, or accessing code without user action.
success_measure: At least 75% of pilot users recover a prior workspace task list from a second browser in under one minute.
monetization: freemium — an offline encrypted journal is free; optional team-shared encrypted handoffs can fund it.
constraints: User-controlled encryption keys; no page-content collection by default; explicit per-origin permissions; support export without a cloud account.
why_distinct: It ports the small operational index around work, rather than competing as another chat or remote IDE.

title: Sampling Budget Coordinator
user: Platform engineers operating multiple OpenTelemetry collectors who need to keep tail-sampling volume within a real fleet-wide budget as instances scale up and down.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A backend engineer describes debugging across logs, traces, dashboards, queues, webhooks, and third-party systems and asks how teams do it in practice.

The adaptive tail sampler enforces goal throughput per collector, allowing N instances to emit up to N times the intended budget; its documented divide-by-instance-count workaround breaks under autoscaling.

recurrence: Cross-system debugging needs traces, while an active collector issue shows that cost-control semantics fail at fleet scale; overruns can multiply storage and vendor spend.
current_workaround: Guess a per-instance fraction, manually divide by replica count, or accept surprise ingestion spikes after autoscaling.
incumbents_and_gap: OpenTelemetry Collector, Grafana Alloy, Datadog, and Honeycomb ingest traces, but their deployment config does not give operators a small independent planner and audit of effective global sampling budget.
smallest_useful_product: A CLI that reads collector configs and replica counts, estimates effective head/tail sampling volume, recommends safe per-instance goals, and emits a deploy-time budget assertion. Non-goals: receiving traces, replacing collectors, or providing an observability backend.
success_measure: Across simulated scale changes, actual exported trace volume stays within 10% of the declared fleet budget in 90% of intervals.
monetization: free — transparent math and deployment adapters are strongest as open infrastructure tooling.
constraints: Make estimates explicit; support only documented processor versions initially; no trace payloads or customer identifiers should be read.
why_distinct: It audits the economics of sampling configuration rather than becoming a telemetry collector or dashboard.

title: Transcript Redaction Gate
user: Teams sharing agent or terminal transcripts with models, support, or CI who need deterministic proof that secrets and configured sensitive patterns are removed before any upload.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An engineer recounts cascading failures in a multi-agent production report pipeline with little visibility and asks for operational war stories.
Gemini CLI users request deterministic redaction because secrets in local transcripts can reach a model before its later redaction step.

recurrence: Production agent workflows generate dense diagnostic records, and a concrete CLI issue identifies secrets reaching a model before redaction; the severity is credential and customer-data exposure.
current_workaround: Trust a model to redact, search text manually, redact after upload, or avoid sharing useful logs entirely.
incumbents_and_gap: Gitleaks, trufflehog, GitHub secret scanning, and vendor memory settings scan repositories or service data; the gap is deterministic, format-aware screening of live transcripts and support bundles before their first external boundary.
smallest_useful_product: An offline CLI/library that recognizes common terminal and JSONL transcript formats, applies policy rules and entropy/credential detectors, produces a redacted copy plus a non-sensitive findings receipt. Non-goals: cloud DLP, model-side redaction, or retaining originals.
success_measure: On a seeded corpus of 200 credentials and identifiers, it blocks 99% of secrets before export while preserving at least 90% of non-secret diagnostic lines.
monetization: one-time — privacy-sensitive teams can evaluate and run a local gate without recurring data fees.
constraints: Offline by default; patterns are advisory and cannot promise complete PII detection; redact output paths; maintain test fixtures without real secrets.
why_distinct: It puts a deterministic privacy boundary before model context, not an LLM-based cleanup step after exposure.

title: Sandbox Capacity Probe
user: Teams running many isolated agent or customer containers who need a repeatable preflight showing whether networking, ports, mounts, and startup latency will remain safe at planned scale.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A builder asks what agent sandboxes are missing while planning templates, queues, output retrieval, and sandbox management through a CLI.
A Docker fleet report traces container-start time growing with published-port count times total host rules, affecting hundreds to thousands of tenant containers.

recurrence: Agent sandbox operators and a concrete multi-tenant Docker fleet report both expose the gap between a working demo and predictable capacity at scale.
current_workaround: Load-test a staging host late, read runtime logs after startup slows, or impose arbitrary container and port limits.
incumbents_and_gap: Docker, Podman, Kubernetes, Testcontainers, and agent-sandbox platforms provision workloads; the gap is a portable local benchmark that translates a sandbox shape into startup, port-rule, mount, and resource-risk evidence.
smallest_useful_product: A CLI that launches bounded synthetic containers against a chosen Docker/Podman host, records startup percentiles and rule counts, and writes a capacity envelope. Non-goals: running untrusted agent code, cluster orchestration, or stress testing third-party systems.
success_measure: For supported hosts, predicted startup p95 at a configured container/port level is within 25% of a subsequent controlled run.
monetization: one-time — capacity planning is periodic and should run inside a customer's own infrastructure.
constraints: Explicit target confirmation and bounded defaults; never benchmark a production host by default; isolate synthetic networks; document runtime-specific results.
why_distinct: It measures the operational envelope of a sandbox design rather than offering another sandbox runtime.

title: Fingerprint Preview
user: Engineers tuning error grouping rules who need to see exactly how a proposed fingerprint would split or merge real incident samples before changing alert volume in production.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An operator says production investigation still requires manual inspection alongside logs and asks how often others face the same debugging workflow.
Sentry users cannot reference visible handled-error stack frames in fingerprint rules, forcing different execution paths into one issue despite available event evidence.

recurrence: Manual production investigation and a concrete error-grouping limitation show a recurring loss of incident signal; bad grouping either hides distinct regressions or floods responders.
current_workaround: Edit server-side rules, wait for new events, inspect raw stacks, and undo the change if groups become noisier.
incumbents_and_gap: Sentry, Bugsnag, Rollbar, and Datadog group errors in their hosted systems; the gap is an offline what-if evaluator that explains group membership against a scrubbed event sample before rule rollout.
smallest_useful_product: A CLI/library that imports redacted event JSON, evaluates a small fingerprint-rule DSL, and reports split/merge deltas with representative frames. Non-goals: error ingestion, alert delivery, or a replacement incident tracker.
success_measure: In a labeled sample, users improve correct grouping precision by 20 percentage points without increasing the number of groups more than 10%.
monetization: free — portable test fixtures and adapters benefit from open adoption; enterprise adapters can be paid later.
constraints: Input must be locally scrubbed; offer vendor-specific parsers but no claim of exact proprietary grouping semantics; preserve stack privacy.
why_distinct: It is a pre-deploy grouping test bench, not a hosted error-monitoring clone.

title: Proxy Policy Rehearsal
user: Self-hosted site operators protecting against abusive automated traffic who need to test reverse-proxy challenge, allowlist, and forwarding rules safely before real users or internal monitors are blocked.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A self-hosting operator asks how to protect low-volume sites from abusive LLM scraping without a CDN and lists firewalls, traps, and CIDR blocks.
An Anubis feature request seeks DNS-based matching so a dynamic uptime-monitor IP list can be allowlisted, showing real policy-management friction.

recurrence: Two independent late-August 2026 self-hosting reports show demand for bot protection but also the risk of brittle allowlists and reverse-proxy policy changes.
current_workaround: Edit proxy expressions or firewall lists in production, temporarily bypass protection, and debug failures from access logs after a monitor or user is blocked.
incumbents_and_gap: Anubis, Cloudflare, Caddy, Nginx, and fail2ban enforce policy; the gap is a local test harness that replays synthetic request/forwarded-header/DNS cases and explains the resulting allow, challenge, or block decision.
smallest_useful_product: A CLI that loads a declarative proxy-policy test file, mocks DNS and request headers, runs selected Anubis/Caddy/Nginx-compatible rule adapters, and emits a readable decision matrix. Non-goals: CAPTCHA service, bot detection feed, CDN, or anti-bot evasion.
success_measure: Before deployment, pilot users catch 90% of seeded monitor/localhost/forwarded-IP policy regressions using the test matrix.
monetization: free — reliable self-hosting policy tests are strongest as transparent community tooling.
constraints: No scraping or bypass features; mock DNS only by default; never collect IP intelligence; adapters must faithfully document unsupported policy semantics.
why_distinct: It rehearses enforcement decisions; it does not become a competing bot firewall or surveillance network.
